title: RFP Team Roles and Responsibilities: How to Build a Proposal Team Structure
summary: What an RFP team is, the core roles and responsibilities, and how to build a proposal team that responds faster and wins more bids.
body_markdown:
## **TL;DR**


- An RFP team is the cross-functional group that owns a company’s RFP responses, usually a proposal manager, writers, SMEs, a compliance lead, and a pricing analyst.
- The core RFP roles and responsibilities split the work: the manager runs the process, writers draft, SMEs supply expertise, compliance checks requirements, and pricing builds the cost model.
- Formalize a proposal team once you handle 10 or more RFPs a month or pursue high-value bids.
- A clear proposal team structure, with one owner per stage, keeps responses consistent and on deadline.
- Track win rate, response time, and content reuse to see whether the structure is working.


## **Introduction**


An RFP team is the cross-functional group that drafts, reviews, and submits a company’s RFP responses. It usually brings together a proposal manager, writers, subject matter experts, a compliance lead, and a pricing analyst, each owning part of the response under a tight deadline.


Having those people is not enough.


To win consistently, a proposal team needs a clear structure, defined roles and responsibilities, and tools that take the guesswork out of the process.[Gallup](https://www.gallup.com/cliftonstrengths/en/278225/how-to-improve-teamwork.aspx) finds that higher team engagement drives 23% higher profitability, and the same discipline applies here: when roles are clear and the team is coordinated, responses get faster and more consistent.


This guide covers what an RFP team is, the core RFP roles and responsibilities, how to structure a proposal team, and the metrics that show it is working.


## **What is an RFP team?**


‍


An RFP team is the cross-functional group a company brings together to respond to a[Request for Proposal](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/what-is-an-rfp-and-key-components-of-an-effective-rfp) . In some organizations, this is a dedicated proposal team. In others, a core proposal function coordinates each bid, while subject-matter experts from sales, legal, finance, product, and technical teams contribute as needed. The people involved may change from one bid to another, while the core team continues managing bids, maintaining the knowledge base, and improving the response process.


That mix of dedicated ownership and cross-functional involvement is central to how RFP teams operate, but it can also make coordination more complex.[PMI](https://www.pmi.org/learning/thought-leadership/pulse/essential-role-communications) found that 56% of the money spent on projects is at risk because of poor communication, and an RFP response has many of the same characteristics: multiple contributors, a shared deadline, and frequent handoffs. The team’s job is to keep those handoffs aligned so the response comes together as one cohesive submission.


That is why clear roles and a shared content library matter more here than in a permanent department. Without them, the same problems repeat on every bid.


## **Core RFP team roles and their responsibilities**


Each role in the response process solves a specific problem, from managing timelines to translating technical details into client-facing value. This section outlines the core team structure, defines what each role does, and explains why it matters in a high-stakes bid environment.


### **1. Proposal manager**


The[proposal manager](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/what-is-proposal-manager) owns the process and the deadline. They build the schedule backward from the due date, assign each section an owner, run the kickoff and a short daily check-in, track status, unblock people, and decide what to cut when time runs short. Because this is a coordination job, keep your strongest writer out of it. A great writer who manages the bid spends the day chasing updates and stops writing the sections that win.


### **2. Proposal writer**


The[proposal writer](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/define-proposal-writing) produces the proposal itself, turning raw input into clear sections that follow the RFP’s structure and the buyer’s criteria. On any bid, they draft several sections, rewrite SME notes and old answers into readable copy, match the tone across parts other people wrote, and fold in edits without breaking the flow. Their hardest job on a team bid is consistency, since five contributors produce five voices. Give one writer final control of the wording so the proposal reads as one person wrote it.


### **3. Subject matter expert (SME)**


The[SME](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/sme-role) supplies the technical depth that makes the response accurate and credible. They answer domain questions from the RFP, review drafts for accuracy, provide diagrams, methods, metrics, and real examples, and correct claims the writer gets slightly wrong. SMEs also have day jobs, which makes them the usual bottleneck. Answer routine questions from your content library first, then send the SME one specific question with context rather than the whole document, and you get an answer in minutes instead of days.


### **4. Graphic designer**


The designer makes the proposal clear to navigate and keeps it on-brand and within the RFP’s formatting rules. They lay out the cover and section templates, turn dense text into tables and timelines, build the one infographic that explains the solution at a glance, and format the document to the exact spec. Evaluators score what they can find quickly, so bring the designer in on day one to shape the structure instead of the night before to decorate a finished draft.


### **5. Executive reviewer**


The executive reviewer is the final approver, judging the proposal on strategy, risk, and fit with company goals. They read the near-final draft, check the win strategy and the commitments the company is making, and either approve it for submission or send it back with clear direction. Protect their time for the one call only they can make, whether this bid is worth the company’s name and resources. When an executive is fixing typos, the earlier reviews failed and the strategic check gets rushed.


### **6. Compliance lead**


The compliance lead makes sure the proposal cannot be thrown out on a technicality. They build and work the requirements matrix line by line, confirm every mandatory form, certification, and attachment is included, enforce page limits, fonts, and file formats, and flag anything missing before submission. Keep this person separate from the writer, because authors read past their own gaps. A fresh reviewer working from the matrix catches the missing attachment or unanswered sub-question that sinks a strong bid.


### **7. Pricing analyst**


The pricing analyst builds the commercial side, a cost model that wins without hurting margin. They model the cost of delivery, pressure-test margins with finance, align with sales on how aggressive to price, and document the assumptions behind every number so the price holds up under questioning. Bring pricing in at kickoff, not at the end. Price often decides the award, and a late number sets off the final-day scramble, because the executive sign-off and the compliance check both wait on it.

## **Why a structured RFP team matters**


A structured RFP team changes what your win rate depends on. Without structure, winning relies on one or two people who know where the content lives and how to write it. When they are busy or unavailable, quality drops. Clear roles and a shared content library spread that knowledge across the team, so every response stays consistent and improves from one bid to the next.


- **Consistency that evaluators notice.** A buying committee reading several vendors spots the response that contradicts itself or changes voice halfway through. When each section has an owner, and everyone works from the same templates and content library, the proposal reads as one coherent answer. That consistency signals a team in control of its process, and it is part of what evaluators score.
- **More capacity without more people.** Clear roles let writing, SME input, and review run in parallel instead of in a queue, and a content library means the team edits proven answers rather than starting from a blank page. The payoff is capacity: the same team can produce more RFP responses without adding headcount.
- **Effort aimed at winnable deals.** Structure also lets a team say no. With a go/no-go step and clear ownership, the team qualifies out bad-fit bids and spends its hours on the ones it can win. Teams without a process tend to answer everything, which spreads them thin and drags win rate down. When the proposal team is aligned with sales, that effort follows the deals that move revenue.


## **How to decide proposal team structure: do it by checking bid size**


Every RFP team has the same simple shape: a proposal manager at the center, with specialists added as the bid needs them. SMEs join only when a question needs them, and the writer and reviewer are always two different people. What changes is how many roles you staff.


Match the structure to your pipeline. Two bids a quarter do not need an enterprise team, and ten a month cannot run on a lean one.


Team size Who is on it Best for


Lean (2 to 3) A manager who also writes, a couple of SMEs, one reviewer Occasional or simple bids


Standard (4 to 6) Manager, writer, SMEs, compliance lead, reviewer A steady flow of mid-size RFPs


Enterprise (7 to 10+) All of the above, plus a capture manager, pricing analyst, designer, and coordinator Large, complex, high-value bids


## **How to build and structure an RFP team? 3 steps**


Before you assign roles, you need to understand when and how to form the right team. The size, scope, and frequency of your RFPs should guide this structure. As your pipeline matures, a formalized team moves from being a nice-to-have to a necessity.


1. **Identifying when to establish a team**


If you’re handling 10+ RFPs monthly, pursuing high-value bids, or struggling with ad hoc coordination, it’s time to formalize your team. Structured teams reduce response time and increase win probability for complex, recurring bids.


1. **Assigning roles and responsibilities**


You already have the role definitions above. Building the team is about matching those roles to your pipeline: run a lean setup for occasional bids, and add specialists as deals get larger and more complex. A[capture manager](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/role-capture-manager) who owns opportunity strategy and a pricing analyst who builds the cost model usually come in once bids get big enough to justify them. Use the structure table above to decide how many roles to staff.


1. **Integrating existing resources**


Map current contributors to formal roles. A sales rep writing key answers might shift into an SME role. An operations manager manually chasing input can transition to a Proposal Coordinator with access to the proper tools.


With the team structure in place, the next step is to clearly define each role’s responsibilities. Understanding who does what ensures accountability and keeps the response process on track.


## **Overcoming challenges in RFP responses**


## **Overcoming RFP Team Challenges**


RFP teams bring together people with different responsibilities, expertise, and priorities. Without clear ownership and coordination, work can overlap, key tasks can be missed, and contributors may receive conflicting instructions. The most common challenges usually come down to unclear roles, fragmented communication, and difficulty coordinating contributors across the response.


- **Unclear ownership:** When responsibilities are not assigned clearly, multiple people may work on the same section while other tasks are overlooked. Defining ownership for each stage and deliverable gives contributors a clear point of responsibility.
- **Fragmented communication:** RFP teams often rely on input from sales, subject-matter experts, legal, finance, product, and other functions. Without clear communication channels and points of contact, updates can get missed and decisions can take longer.
- **Late SME input:** Subject-matter experts may have limited availability alongside their regular responsibilities. Setting clear deadlines and identifying backup contributors early helps the proposal team avoid delays when critical input is needed.
- **Overlapping responsibilities:** Some tasks require input from several functions, but shared responsibility can become unclear ownership. Documenting who leads, reviews, approves, and contributes to each task helps prevent duplication and gaps.
- **Version control issues:** Multiple contributors working from different drafts can introduce conflicting edits and outdated information. A shared working document or centralized platform gives the team a common source of truth.
- **Inconsistent responses:** Different contributors may answer similar questions using different terminology, outdated information, or conflicting claims. A maintained knowledge base and clear review responsibilities help keep responses consistent.
- **Last-minute coordination:** Tight deadlines leave less time to resolve unanswered questions, collect approvals, or reconcile conflicting inputs. A defined response timeline with internal deadlines gives the team time to resolve issues before submission.


When roles, ownership, and handoffs are clear, RFP teams can spend less time coordinating the response and more time improving its quality.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Who should be on an RFP response team?


An RFP response team typically includes a proposal manager, proposal writer, subject matter experts, and reviewers. Depending on the bid, the team may also include sales, legal, compliance, finance, pricing, design, and technical specialists. The exact mix depends on the RFP’s complexity, value, and requirements.


### What does an RFP proposal manager do?


An RFP proposal manager owns the response process from kickoff to submission. They build the timeline, assign responsibilities, coordinate contributors, track progress, manage reviews, and keep the response aligned with the RFP requirements and deadline.


### What is the role of an SME in an RFP response?


A subject matter expert provides specialized knowledge that the proposal team may not have. SMEs answer technical or domain-specific questions, review responses for accuracy, and provide supporting details, examples, and evidence.


### How many people should be on an RFP team?


There is no fixed team size. A simple RFP may need two or three people, while complex or high-value bids can require seven or more contributors across proposal management, writing, technical, compliance, pricing, design, and executive review. The team should match the size and complexity of the bid.


### Who is responsible for writing an RFP response?


The proposal writer or proposal team usually owns the written response, while SMEs, sales, product, technical, legal, and other contributors provide the information needed for specific sections. In smaller teams, one person may handle both proposal management and writing.


### How do you assign roles and responsibilities for an RFP?


Start by breaking the RFP into its major requirements and deliverables. Assign one clear owner to each section or task, then identify who needs to contribute, review, or approve it. A responsibility matrix can help make these assignments visible across the team.


### What is the difference between an RFP team and a proposal team?


The terms are often used interchangeably for the vendor-side team responding to an RFP. An RFP team may include everyone contributing to a specific response, while a proposal team can also refer to the core function responsible for managing multiple bids and the broader proposal process.


### When should a company create a dedicated proposal team?


A dedicated proposal function becomes more useful when a company handles a steady volume of RFPs, pursues high-value bids, or spends significant time coordinating contributors. Companies with fewer or simpler bids may use a smaller team with people taking on multiple roles.
